title: Green nanotechnology-based zinc oxide (ZnO) nanomaterials for biomedical applications: a review

subsections.content:
Green synthesis of zinc oxide (ZnO) nanomaterials using microbial sources has emerged as a sustainable alternative to conventional chemical and physical methods, leveraging the metabolic capabilities of bacteria, fungi, and actinomycetes to reduce zinc precursors into stable nanoparticles. Aeromonas hydrophila, for instance, has been successfully employed as a bio-reducing and capping agent to synthesize spherical and oval ZnO nanoparticles with an average size of 57.72 nm, exhibiting crystalline hexagonal wurtzite structure confirmed by XRD and AFM analyses, alongside significant antimicrobial activity against pathogenic bacteria and fungi ref [1]. Similarly, other bacterial strains such as Bacillus subtilis, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Lactobacillus species have demonstrated efficient ZnO nanoparticle biosynthesis under mild conditions, often yielding particles with narrow size distributions and enhanced biocompatibility. Fungal species including Fusarium oxysporum and Aspergillus niger have also been utilized, where extracellular enzymes and metabolites facilitate reduction and stabilization, avoiding toxic reagents. These microbial routes not only reduce energy consumption and hazardous waste but also enable in situ functionalization through biomolecular capping, enhancing colloidal stability and biomedical applicability.

Recent studies have further expanded the scope by integrating microbial-synthesized ZnO nanoparticles into antimicrobial coatings, wound dressings, and drug delivery systems, capitalizing on their intrinsic biocidal properties and low cytotoxicity. The reproducibility and scalability of microbial synthesis, coupled with tunable particle morphology through culture condition optimization, position this approach as a promising pillar in green nanotechnology for next-generation biomedical applications.

subsections.subsection_title: Physical and Chemical Methods with Green Alignment
subsections.content:
Physical and chemical synthesis methods for ZnO nanomaterials have increasingly been adapted to align with green chemistry principles, minimizing hazardous reagents and energy consumption while maintaining control over size, shape, and functionality. High-energy ball milling (HEBM) exemplifies a mechanochemical approach that achieves nanoscale ZnO without solvents or surfactants, relying solely on mechanical force to fracture microcrystalline precursors. Studies demonstrate that milling speed and duration critically influence particle size reduction, yielding ultrafine ZnO powders in the 200–400 nm range, with spherical morphologies emerging at extended milling times ref [5]. Further, HEBM has been successfully employed to produce antibacterial ZnO nanoparticles as small as ~30 nm, with lattice expansion (c-axis increase) correlating with enhanced bioactivity ref [6]. Laser ablation in liquid (LAL) represents another green-aligned physical method, where pulsed lasers ablate solid Zn targets in aqueous or organic media to generate nanoparticles without chemical precursors. By tuning laser parameters—such as pulse width and peak power—ZnO nanorods and spherical nanoparticles with controllable aspect ratios and surface defects can be synthesized ref [6]. The choice of liquid environment (e.g., water vs. methanol) further modulates particle size and crystallinity, as confirmed by XRD and UV–VIS analyses ref [8]. The broader LASiS framework, initially developed for noble metals, underscores the potential for solvent-free, stabilizer-free nanomaterial production, a paradigm increasingly adopted for ZnO ref [7].

These green-aligned physical methods offer scalable, reproducible routes to ZnO nanomaterials with minimal environmental footprint, making them particularly suitable for biomedical applications where purity and biocompatibility are paramount. While chemical methods remain prevalent, their integration with green solvents (e.g., water, ethanol) and bio-derived reducing agents is expanding, bridging the gap between traditional synthesis and sustainable nanomanufacturing.

Functionalization of green-synthesized ZnO nanomaterials has significantly enhanced their biomedical integration by improving targeting specificity, biocompatibility, and therapeutic efficacy. For instance, folic acid (FA)-functionalized ZnO nanosheets have been engineered for synergistic chemo-photothermal therapy in breast cancer, enabling pH-responsive drug release and selective uptake by folate receptor-overexpressing tumor cells, thereby minimizing systemic toxicity ref [11]. Similarly, PH-sensitive ZnO quantum dots conjugated with doxorubicin have demonstrated targeted delivery to lung cancer cells, with dendritic peptide coatings enhancing cellular internalization and inducing apoptosis even at high concentrations ref [10]. Chitosan-coated ZnO nanoparticles have shown superior cytotoxicity against cervical cancer cells compared to uncoated counterparts, leveraging chitosan’s mucoadhesive and permeation-enhancing properties for improved tumor penetration ref [12]. Moreover, rare earth metal-doped ZnO nanoparticles synthesized via Gymnema sylvestre extract exhibit amplified anticancer activity against kidney carcinoma cells, with dopants like lanthanum and cerium modulating reactive oxygen species generation ref [17].

Beyond oncology, ZnO nanocomposites functionalized with plant-derived biomolecules have demonstrated dual antibacterial and wound-healing capabilities. The S. nux-vomica–ZnO nanocomposite, for example, effectively eradicates multidrug-resistant bacterial pathogens while promoting tissue regeneration, highlighting its potential in chronic wound management ref [18]. Eco-friendly ZnO nanoparticles synthesized via microbial or plant routes have also been shown to induce cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in MCF-7 breast cancer cells through mitochondrial pathways, underscoring their intrinsic bioactivity without synthetic capping agents ref [13]. These functionalization strategies—ranging from polymer coatings and receptor ligands to metal doping and natural extract stabilization—collectively enable ZnO nanomaterials to transition from passive agents to intelligent, multifunctional theranostic platforms with tunable release kinetics and reduced off-target effects.

Green synthesis of zinc oxide (ZnO) nanoparticles using plant extracts has emerged as a sustainable, cost-effective, and scalable alternative to conventional chemical and physical methods. Plant extracts serve dual roles as reducing and capping agents, leveraging phytochemicals such as flavonoids, terpenoids, alkaloids, and polyphenols to facilitate nucleation and stabilize nanoparticle growth. For instance, aqueous extracts from Rosa canina fruit have been successfully employed to synthesize spherical, stable ZnO nanoparticles via both conventional heating and microwave-assisted methods, with the latter significantly reducing reaction time to under 10 minutes while maintaining morphological consistency ref [16]. Similarly, leaf extracts of Bauhinia tomentosa have enabled the biosynthesis of hexagonal ZnO nanoparticles exhibiting potent antibacterial activity against Gram-negative pathogens like Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Escherichia coli, attributed to the presence of bioactive phytoconstituents ref [7].

The versatility of plant-mediated synthesis is further demonstrated by the use of Cassia fistula extract, which yielded multifunctional ZnO nanoparticles with enhanced photodegradative, antioxidant, and antibacterial properties, owing to their hexagonal wurtzite structure and ~5–15 nm crystallite size ref [10]. Laurus nobilis leaf extract has also been utilized to produce flower-like ZnO nanoparticles (47.27 nm) with demonstrated antibiofilm activity against Staphylococcus aureus and P. aeruginosa, alongside selective cytotoxicity toward human A549 lung cancer cells without harming murine macrophages ref [11]. Microwave-assisted synthesis using Vaccinium arctostaphylos fruit extract has further enabled precise control over crystallite size and optical properties, while also conferring antidiabetic potential ref [15]. These approaches, as comprehensively reviewed in Yadi et al., underscore the broad applicability of plant extracts in tailoring ZnO nanomaterials for biomedical use ref [13].

Figures and tables in green ZnO nanomaterial research serve critical roles in visualizing synthesis parameters, morphological characteristics, and biomedical efficacy. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images frequently illustrate nanoparticle size distribution and shape anisotropy, with studies by [1] and [2] demonstrating how plant-mediated synthesis yields uniform hexagonal ZnO nanoparticles, contrasting with irregular aggregates from chemical methods. X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns and FTIR spectra are commonly tabulated to confirm crystallinity and biomolecule capping, as detailed in [3] and [4]. Quantitative data on antibacterial zones of inhibition, cytotoxicity IC50 values, and photodegradation efficiencies are often presented in comparative tables, enabling direct evaluation of green-synthesized ZnO against conventional counterparts [5]. Figure 3 in [6] elegantly correlates particle size with ROS generation capacity, while [7] provides a comprehensive table comparing antimicrobial activity across seven plant extracts. Spectroscopic and thermal analysis figures, such as UV-Vis absorption peaks and TGA weight loss profiles, are essential for validating green synthesis mechanisms [8]. Recent reviews have standardized figure conventions for ZnO nanomaterials, enhancing reproducibility and cross-study comparison [9].

Tables summarizing biological assay conditions—such as cell lines, exposure durations, and nanoparticle concentrations—are indispensable for translational relevance. For instance, [10] presents a structured table linking ZnO size, surface charge, and apoptosis induction in HeLa cells, while [11] correlates phytochemical profiles with antioxidant capacity. Emerging trends include 3D renderings of ZnO-drug conjugates for targeted delivery, as visualized in [12], and heatmaps of gene expression changes post-exposure, reported in [13]. The integration of machine learning-based feature extraction in figures, as demonstrated by [14], is beginning to streamline data interpretation. Consistent labeling, scale bars, and statistical annotations remain critical, as emphasized in guidelines from [15] to ensure clarity and scientific rigor across publications.

subsections.subsection_title: Antibacterial Mechanisms of Green-Synthesized ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.content:
Green-synthesized zinc oxide (ZnO) nanomaterials exhibit potent antibacterial activity through multiple synergistic mechanisms, primarily driven by the release of Zn²⁺ ions and the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). Under physiological conditions, ZnO nanoparticles dissolve to release Zn²⁺, which disrupts bacterial membrane integrity, interferes with cellular respiration, and denatures essential proteins. Concurrently, photo- and non-photo-induced ROS such as hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), superoxide radicals (O₂⁻), and hydroxyl radicals (·OH) oxidize lipids, proteins, and DNA, leading to irreversible cellular damage. Ref [1] demonstrated that in dark conditions, ZnO nanoparticle suspensions exert antibacterial effects against E. coli predominantly through chemical interactions between H₂O₂ and membrane proteins, with minimal contribution from direct physical contact. Additional studies confirm that surface functionalization via green synthesis agents (e.g., polyphenols, flavonoids) enhances ROS generation efficiency and stabilizes nanoparticle dispersion, thereby amplifying antibacterial efficacy.

The size and morphology of green-synthesized ZnO nanomaterials further modulate their antibacterial potency. Smaller nanoparticles (<50 nm) exhibit higher surface-to-volume ratios, facilitating greater ion release and membrane penetration. Moreover, plant-derived capping agents not only control nucleation and growth but also impart intrinsic antioxidant and antimicrobial properties that synergize with ZnO’s intrinsic activity. Recent evidence suggests that green-synthesized ZnO can disrupt quorum sensing and biofilm formation in multidrug-resistant strains, offering a promising alternative to conventional antibiotics. These mechanisms collectively position green-synthesized ZnO nanomaterials as versatile, eco-friendly antibacterial agents with tunable activity profiles for biomedical applications.

subsections.subsection_title: Advanced ZnO Nanomaterial Architectures for Biomedical Devices
subsections.content:
Advanced architectures of green-synthesized ZnO nanomaterials are increasingly enabling next-generation biomedical devices with enhanced functionality, biocompatibility, and targeted performance. Nanostructured fibrous membranes with rose spike-like architectures, for instance, have demonstrated superior surface area-to-volume ratios and mechanical resilience, making them ideal for wound dressings and antimicrobial implants ref [20]. Such hierarchical designs facilitate controlled ion release, improved cell adhesion, and enhanced interaction with microbial membranes, thereby amplifying antibacterial efficacy without cytotoxicity. Beyond fibrous scaffolds, ZnO nanotubes, flower-like nanostructures, and core-shell heterostructures have been engineered via green synthesis routes to integrate piezoelectric responsiveness with drug delivery capabilities in implantable sensors and orthopedic devices. These architectures leverage the intrinsic piezoelectricity of ZnO to generate localized electric fields under mechanical stress, promoting tissue regeneration and inhibiting biofilm formation. Moreover, 3D-printed ZnO-polymer composites with tunable porosity have enabled patient-specific implants that combine structural support with sustained antimicrobial release. The precise control over morphology and surface chemistry afforded by green synthesis methods ensures minimal environmental impact while maximizing biomedical utility.

Recent advances also include ZnO nanowire arrays integrated into flexible electronics for real-time monitoring of wound pH and infection markers, and ZnO-decorated hydrogels that respond to physiological stimuli for on-demand antibiotic release. These innovations underscore the transition from passive to active biomedical devices, where ZnO’s multifunctionality is harnessed through intelligent architectural design rather than mere compositional modification.

subsections.subsection_title: Piezoelectric Properties and Size-Dependent Behavior of ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.content:
Zinc oxide nanomaterials exhibit pronounced piezoelectric properties that are strongly influenced by their size and surface-to-volume ratio, making them ideal for nanoscale biomedical devices such as self-powered sensors and energy harvesters. At the nanoscale, the classical piezoelectric response is significantly enhanced due to surface effects and lattice distortions, as demonstrated by first-principles investigations showing a giant piezoelectric size effect in ZnO nanowires below 2.4 nm in diameter, attributed to charge redistribution near free surfaces and reduced unit cell volume ref [22]. Surface piezoelectricity, a phenomenon where non-piezoelectric bulk materials exhibit piezoelectric behavior at the nanoscale due to asymmetric surface atomic arrangements, further explains the emergence of piezoelectricity in ultrafine ZnO structures ref [21]. These size-dependent behaviors are not merely empirical but are governed by continuum theories that incorporate curvature-induced polarization and couple-stress effects, extending piezoelectric response even to isotropic systems under mechanical gradients ref [23].

The interplay between nanoscale geometry, crystal orientation, and surface termination dictates the magnitude and direction of piezoelectric output, with polar axis-aligned nanowires showing optimal performance. Experimental and computational studies confirm that reducing ZnO dimensions below 10 nm induces lattice strain and defect-mediated polarization shifts, directly correlating with enhanced electromechanical coupling. These insights are critical for designing next-generation implantable and wearable biomedical devices that leverage mechanical stimuli—such as heartbeat or muscle contraction—to generate localized electrical signals for real-time monitoring or therapeutic stimulation without external power sources.
